entries.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
entries.lesson_core_move: State the value-based definition of the unit step function and interpret it as the basic continuous-time on-off signal used to build shifted, delayed, and rectangular-pulse signal descriptions.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Unit Step Before and After the Switch

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate $u(-0.1)$ and $u(8)$ with the definition from the tutorial.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $-0.1<0$, the unit step is off there, so $u(-0.1)=0$. Because $8>0$, the unit step is on there, so $u(8)=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate $u(10)$ and $u(-7)$ with the definition from the tutorial.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $10>0$, the unit step is on there, so $u(10)=1$. Because $-7<0$, the unit step is off there, so $u(-7)=0$.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Unit Step at the Switching Time

prompt_blocks.text: Under this lesson convention, what are the values of $u(-0.01)$, $u(0)$, and $u(0.01)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Negative time is off, so $u(-0.01)=0$. The lesson convention sets the switching time to the on value, so $u(0)=1$. Positive time is also on, so $u(0.01)=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement correctly describes the boundary-time value under this lesson convention?

choice_blocks.text: $u(0)=1$, so it matches $u(0.01)$ and differs from $u(-0.01)$
$u(0)=0$, so it matches $u(-0.01)$ and differs from $u(0.01)$
$u(0)=\frac{1}{2}$, so it sits halfway between the left and right values
$u(0)=1$, so it matches $u(-0.01)$ and differs from $u(0.01)$
$u(0)=0$, so both nearby values are also $0$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lesson convention assigns the switch instant to the on value, so $u(0)=1$. The nearby positive time $0.01$ is also on, while the nearby negative time $-0.01$ is off.

sections.section_title: Reading the Unit Step Function from a Time-Axis Graph

image_slots.image_description: A minimal time-axis graph of a unit step with a single jump at t=0. The graph is 0 for t<0 and 1 for t>=0. Include clear axis labels and a visible switch marker at 0.
A minimal time-axis graph of a unit step with a single jump at t=2. The graph is 0 for t<2 and 1 for t>=2. Include clear axis labels and a visible switch marker at 2.

prompt_blocks.text: From the graph, identify $u(-3)$, $u(0)$, and the interval where the signal is on.

choice_blocks.text: $u(-3)=0$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 0$.
$u(-3)=1$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t<0$.
$u(-3)=0$, $u(0)=0$, and the signal is on for $t>0$.
$u(-3)=0$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\le 0$.
$u(-3)=0.5$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 0$.

questions.correct_answer: $u(-3)=0$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph switches at $t=0$, so $t=-3$ is left of the jump and gives $0$. At the switching time, the lesson convention gives $u(0)=1$.
Therefore the signal is on for $t\ge 0$, which matches choice A.

prompt_blocks.text: From the graph, identify $u(1)$, $u(2)$, and the interval where the signal is on.

choice_blocks.text: $u(1)=0$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 2$.
$u(1)=1$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t<2$.
$u(1)=0$, $u(2)=0$, and the signal is on for $t>2$.
$u(1)=0$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 0$.
$u(1)=0.5$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\le 2$.

questions.correct_answer: $u(1)=0$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph switches at $t=2$, so $t=1$ is left of the jump and gives $0$. At the switching time, the lesson convention gives $u(2)=1$.
Therefore the signal is on for $t\ge 2$, which matches choice A.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Recognizing the Unit Step as the Basic Continuous-Time Switching Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise signal matches $x(t)u(t)$ when $x(t)=t^2$?

choice_blocks.text: It shifts the signal in phase instead of turning it on and off in time.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The unit step is the right-side gate: $u(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $u(t)=1$ for $t\ge0$ under the lesson convention. So multiplying by $u(t)$ kills the left side and leaves $t^2$ unchanged on the right side.

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise signal matches $x(t)u(t)$ when $x(t)=3t-1$?

choice_blocks.text: It changes the signal's phase instead of gating its amplitude.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same gate applies here: $u(t)$ is off for $t<0$ and on for $t\ge0$. So the product suppresses $3t-1$ on the left side and passes it through unchanged on the right side.

entries.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret x(t)u(t) as using the unit step as an on-off switch that suppresses a continuous-time signal before t = 0 and passes it afterward, supporting construction of started, delayed, and pulsed signals with unit steps.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
sections.section_title: Evaluating x(t)u(t) Before t = 0

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=x(t)u(t)$ with $x(t)=t^2+1$, evaluate $y(-4)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Since $-4<0$, the unit step is off, so $u(-4)=0$.
Even though $x(-4)=(-4)^2+1=17$, the product is $y(-4)=17\cdot 0=0$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=x(t)u(t)$ with $x(t)=2t-7$, evaluate $y(-3)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $-3<0$, the switch is off and $u(-3)=0$.
So even though $x(-3)=2(-3)-7=-13$, the product is $y(-3)=-13\cdot 0=0$.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
sections.section_title: Evaluating x(t)u(t) After t = 0

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=(4t-5)u(t)$, what is $y(2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $2>0$, this is in the on region, so $u(2)=1$. Then $y(2)=(4\cdot2-5)\cdot1=3$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=\left(\frac{3}{2}t+1\right)u(t)$, what is $y(4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $4>0$, this is in the on region, so $u(4)=1$. Then $y(4)=\left(\frac{3}{2}\cdot4+1\right)\cdot1=7$.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
sections.section_title: Writing the On-Off Output of x(t)u(t) in Piecewise Form

prompt_blocks.text: Write $y(t)=(5-2t)u(t)$ in piecewise form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The unit step is off for $t<0$, so the output is $0$ there.
At and after $t=0$, the step is on, so the output equals the active formula $5-2t$.

prompt_blocks.text: Write $z(t)=(t^2-4)u(t)$ in piecewise form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $t<0$, the unit step is off, so the output is $0$.
For $t\ge 0$, the unit step passes the signal through unchanged, so the active branch is $t^2-4$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Translate shifted unit step functions into exact switch-on times on the continuous-time axis so they can be used to start, delay, and construct signals compactly.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Finding the Switch-On Time from u(t - T)

prompt_blocks.text: Find the switch-on time of $y(t)=u(t-6)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A shifted unit step turns on when its argument is zero. Set $t-6=0$ and solve to get $t=6$.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the switch-on time of $x(t)=u(t-2)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The switch-on time is where the argument of the unit step equals zero. Set $t-2=0$ and solve to get $t=2$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Finding the Switch-On Time from u(t + T)

prompt_blocks.text: What is the switch-on time of $y(t)=u(t+8)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the inside of the unit step to zero: $t+8=0$. Solving gives $t=-8$, so the plus sign inside the step means the switch happens at the opposite sign.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=u(t+6)$, which piecewise description is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the inside of the unit step to zero: $t+6=0$. That gives $t=-6$, so the signal is off for $t<-6$ and on for $t\ge -6$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Finding the Switch-On Time from u(t - t0)

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=u(t-t_0)$ with $t_0=4$, what is the switch-on time?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the inside argument equal to zero: $t-t_0=0$. For $u(t-t_0)$, the switch-on time is always $t=t_0$, so with $t_0=4$ the switch-on time is $t=4$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=u(t-t_0)$ with $t_0=-2$, what is the switch-on time?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same rule again: set the argument to zero, $t-t_0=0$. The switch-on time equals the parameter, so when $t_0=-2$ the function switches on at $t=-2$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Placing Shifted Unit Steps on the Time Axis

prompt_blocks.text: Order the switch-on times of $y_1(t)=u(t-4)$, $y_2(t)=u(t+2)$, and $y_3(t)=u(t-1)$ from earliest to latest.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $y_2(t)=u(t+2)$ switches on at $t=-2$, $y_3(t)=u(t-1)$ switches on at $t=1$, and $y_1(t)=u(t-4)$ switches on at $t=4$. So the earliest-to-latest order is $y_2(t), y_3(t), y_1(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Order the switch-on times of $z_1(t)=u(t-1)$, $z_2(t)=u(t+5)$, and $z_3(t)=u(t-3)$ from earliest to latest.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $z_2(t)=u(t+5)$ switches on at $t=-5$, $z_1(t)=u(t-1)$ switches on at $t=1$, and $z_3(t)=u(t-3)$ switches on at $t=3$. So the earliest-to-latest order is $z_2(t), z_1(t), z_3(t)$.

entries.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a zero-before-start continuous-time signal from piecewise form into a step-gated expression by multiplying the active formula by the unit step that turns on at the start time.

sections.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Starting an Active Formula at t = 0

prompt_blocks.text: Convert the piecewise signal into an equivalent unit-step expression: $x(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $x(t)=3t-2$ for $t\ge 0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The switch starts at $t=0$, so the gate is $u(t)$. Keep the active formula unchanged and multiply it by the step: $x(t)=(3t-2)u(t)$. For $t<0$, the step is $0$, so the signal is zero before the start.

prompt_blocks.text: Convert the piecewise signal into an equivalent unit-step expression: $y(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $y(t)=t^2+4$ for $t\ge 0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The start time is still $0$, so the gate is $u(t)$. Multiply the active branch by that gate without changing the branch itself: $y(t)=(t^2+4)u(t)$. That makes the signal zero for $t<0$ and preserves the active formula for $t\ge 0$.

sections.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Starting an Active Formula After t = 0

prompt_blocks.text: Convert $x(t)=0$ for $t<3$ and $x(t)=e^{-t}$ for $t\ge 3$ to a unit-step expression.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The switch is at $t=3$, so the gate is $u(t-3)$. Keep the active formula as $e^{-t}$ and multiply it by that step, giving $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t-3)$. The other choices either miss the delayed switch, shift the formula itself, flip the step, or ignore the inactive interval.

prompt_blocks.text: Convert $x(t)=0$ for $t<\frac{1}{2}$ and $x(t)=t^2+1$ for $t\ge \frac{1}{2}$ to a unit-step expression.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The switch occurs at $t=\frac{1}{2}$, so the gate is $u(t-\frac{1}{2})$. Keep the active formula exactly as $t^2+1$ and multiply it by the step, which gives $x(t)=(t^2+1)u(t-\frac{1}{2})$. The other choices either shift the formula unnecessarily, leave the gate unshifted, flip the step, or omit the switch entirely.

sections.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Starting an Active Formula Before t = 0

prompt_blocks.text: Convert $x(t)=0$ for $t<-2$ and $x(t)=\cos(t)$ for $t\ge -2$ into a unit-step expression.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The start time is $-2$, so the gate must turn on with $u(t+2)$. Keep the active branch unchanged and multiply it by the gate, giving $x(t)=\cos(t)u(t+2)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Convert $x(t)=0$ for $t<-3$ and $x(t)=3e^{-t}$ for $t\ge -3$ into a unit-step expression.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The start time is $-3$, so the gate is $u(t+3)$. Keep the active formula exactly as $3e^{-t}$ and multiply it by the gate to get $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t+3)$.

entries.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a delayed exponential into the correct unit-step form e^{a(t - t0)}u(t - t0), recognizing how the shifted step turns the signal on at t0 while the exponential's argument sets the delayed time origin.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Delaying a Basic Exponential to a Positive Start Time

prompt_blocks.text: Convert $x(t)=e^{-3t}$ for $t\ge 2$ and $0$ otherwise into unit-step form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The delay is $2$, so every $t$ in the prototype becomes $t-2$. The step must turn the signal on at the same time, so the matching form is $x(t)=e^{-3(t-2)}u(t-2)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Convert $x(t)=e^{-t}$ for $t\ge 5$ and $0$ otherwise into unit-step form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal starts at $t=5$, so the delay shifts both the exponential argument and the step by $5$. That gives $x(t)=e^{-(t-5)}u(t-5)$.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Including Scale Factors in Delayed Exponential Signals

prompt_blocks.text: Convert $x(t)=4e^{-0.5t}$ delayed by $2$ into unit-step form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay of $2$ changes the time argument to $t-2$ in both the exponential and the unit step. The gain $4$ stays outside as a separate multiplier.

prompt_blocks.text: Convert $x(t)=2e^{0.5t}$ delayed by $4$ into unit-step form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay of $4$ shifts the time reference to $t-4$ in both the exponential and the unit step. The coefficient $2$ remains outside, and the positive exponent stays positive after the delay.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Converting Piecewise Delayed Exponentials to Step Form

prompt_blocks.text: Convert the piecewise signal $x(t)=\{e^{-t},\,3\le t<8;\,0,\,\text{elsewhere}\}$ to step form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Re-anchor the exponential at the start time $t=3$: $e^{-t}=e^{-3}e^{-(t-3)}$. The gate must be $u(t-3)-u(t-8)$ so the signal turns on at $3$ and off at $8$.

prompt_blocks.text: Convert the piecewise signal $x(t)=\{e^{-2t},\,2\le t<7;\,0,\,\text{elsewhere}\}$ to step form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Re-anchor at the start time $t=2$: $e^{-2t}=e^{-4}e^{-2(t-2)}$. The step difference $u(t-2)-u(t-7)$ keeps the signal on only for $2\le t<7$.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Distinguishing Delayed Exponentials from Gated Unshifted Exponentials

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression matches a signal that equals $e^{2t}$ for $1 \le t < 5$ and $0$ elsewhere, while keeping the waveform unshifted?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The waveform is already written as $e^{2t}$ in global time, so the exponent stays unshifted. The finite interval comes only from the step difference.
A delayed form would move the time origin inside the exponential, which is not what this prompt asks for.

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression matches a signal that equals $e^{-3t}$ for $4 \le t < 9$ and $0$ elsewhere, without re-anchoring the exponential?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The exponential is already given as $e^{-3t}$ in global time, so it should not be re-anchored. The step difference alone gates the active interval from $t=4$ to $t=9$.
Any choice that shifts the exponent is turning the waveform into a delayed signal instead of a gated unshifted one.

entries.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
entries.lesson_core_move: Construct rectangular pulses by subtracting appropriately shifted unit step functions to switch a chosen amplitude on at the leading edge and off at the trailing edge.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Creating a Unit-Height Pulse from t = 0 to t = T

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression gives a unit-height pulse that is on from $t=0$ to $t=3$ and zero elsewhere?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The first step turns the pulse on at $t=0$ and the delayed step turns it off at $t=3$, so the unit-height pulse is $u(t)-u(t-3)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression gives a unit-height pulse that is on from $t=0$ to $t=5$ and zero elsewhere?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The on-switch is $u(t)$ and the off-switch is the delayed step $u(t-5)$, so the pulse is $u(t)-u(t-5)$.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Moving the Pulse Window to Start at t = a

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression is the unit-height pulse that is 1 on $[a,a+4]$ and zero elsewhere?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pulse should turn on at $t=a$ and turn off 4 units later at $t=a+4$. The shifted-step difference that does that is $u(t-a)-u(t-a-4)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression is the unit-height pulse that is 1 on $[-2,2]$ and zero elsewhere?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A start time of $-2$ means the leading edge is at $t=-2$, so the on-switch is $u(t+2)$. Four time units later, the pulse turns off at $t=2$, so the off-switch is $u(t-2)$.
Subtracting those shifted steps gives the unit-height pulse on $[-2,2]$: $u(t+2)-u(t-2)$.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Scaling the Pulse to a Chosen Amplitude

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression gives a pulse of height $5$ on $[1,4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval is still $[1,4)$, so the step difference is $u(t-1)-u(t-4)$. Putting $5$ in front of the whole difference makes the plateau height $5$; the other choices either drop the coefficient, move the off-switch, change the width, or flip the sign.

prompt_blocks.text: Which expression gives a pulse of height $-4$ on $[1,4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The step difference still controls the window $[1,4)$, and the leading coefficient sets the height. Multiplying the entire difference by $-4$ gives a pulse whose plateau is $-4$; the other choices either use the wrong sign, wrong off-switch, wrong width, or no coefficient at all.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Writing a Rectangular Pulse from Its Height and Endpoints

prompt_blocks.text: A pulse has height $5$ from $t=-3$ to $t=1$. Write the expression in unit-step form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The left endpoint $t=-3$ becomes $u(t+3)$, and the right endpoint $t=1$ becomes $u(t-1)$. Put the height $5$ in front of the full difference, so the pulse is $5[u(t+3)-u(t-1)]$.

prompt_blocks.text: A pulse has height $2$ from $t=0$ to $t=4$. Write the expression in unit-step form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The left endpoint $t=0$ gives $u(t)$, and the right endpoint $t=4$ gives $u(t-4)$. Multiply the whole difference by the height $2$, so the pulse is $2[u(t)-u(t-4)]$.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Reading the On and Off Times from a Step-Difference Pulse

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=3[u(t+3)-u(t-1)]$, which option gives the correct non-zero interval and level?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The first step turns the pulse on at $t=-3$ because $u(t+3)=u(t-(-3))$, and the second step turns it off at $t=1$. The coefficient 3 sets the plateau height, so the signal is 3 on $-3 \le t < 1$ and 0 elsewhere.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=4[u(t-2)-u(t-7)]$, which option gives the correct non-zero interval and level?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The first step turns the pulse on at $t=2$, the second step turns it off at $t=7$, and the coefficient 4 sets the level. So the signal is 4 on $2 \le t < 7$ and 0 elsewhere.
